subject: Physics
text: Differentiate between scalar and vector quantities. Give one example of each.
modelAnswer: Scalar quantity: has only magnitude, no direction. Example: mass, speed, time, distance. Vector quantity: has both magnitude and direction. Example: force, velocity, displacement, acceleration.
keyPoints: Scalar: magnitude only (speed, mass, temperature)
Vector: magnitude + direction (velocity, force, displacement)
Speed is scalar; velocity is vector (same magnitude, different concept)

subject: Physics
text: A ray of light enters a glass prism from air. (a) State the condition for total internal reflection. (b) How does the critical angle depend on the refractive index of the medium? (c) Name one application of total internal reflection.
modelAnswer: (a) Conditions: (i) light must travel from denser to rarer medium, (ii) the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle. (b) Critical angle (C) is related to refractive index (n): n = 1/sin C. As refractive index increases, critical angle decreases. (c) Applications: optical fibres, periscopes, binoculars, diamonds (sparkle).
keyPoints: TIR: denser→rarer medium AND angle of incidence > critical angle
n = 1/sin C (higher n → smaller critical angle)
Applications: optical fibres, diamonds, periscopes, prisms in binoculars

subject: Physics
text: (a) Define forced vibrations. (b) Distinguish between forced vibrations and resonance.
modelAnswer: (a) Forced vibrations: vibrations produced in a body by an external periodic force of a frequency different from the natural frequency of the body. The body vibrates at the frequency of the external force. (b) Forced vibrations: body vibrates at external force's frequency (not its own). Resonance: a special case of forced vibrations where the frequency of external force equals the natural frequency of the body, causing maximum amplitude.
keyPoints: Forced vibrations: external force drives body at external frequency
Resonance: external frequency = natural frequency → maximum amplitude
Resonance is special/extreme case of forced vibrations

subject: Physics
text: Distinguish between heat capacity and specific heat capacity. A body of mass 2 kg absorbs 4200 J of heat energy and its temperature rises by 5°C. Calculate its specific heat capacity.
modelAnswer: Heat capacity: quantity of heat needed to raise temperature of the whole body by 1°C (unit: J/°C or J/K). Specific heat capacity: quantity of heat needed to raise temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1°C (unit: J/kg°C). Calculation: Q = mcΔT → c = Q/(mΔT) = 4200/(2×5) = 4200/10 = 420 J/kg°C.
keyPoints: Heat capacity = Q/ΔT (for whole body); unit J/°C
Specific heat capacity = Q/(m×ΔT) (per kg); unit J/kg°C

subject: Physics
text: (a) Define mechanical advantage (MA) of a machine. (b) A machine has a velocity ratio of 5 and efficiency of 80%. Calculate its mechanical advantage.
modelAnswer: (a) Mechanical Advantage (MA) = Load / Effort. It is the ratio of load (output force) to effort (input force) applied to a machine. (b) MA = Efficiency × VR = (80/100) × 5 = 0.8 × 5 = 4.
keyPoints: MA = Load / Effort
MA = Efficiency × VR = (η/100) × VR

subject: Physics
text: Three resistors of 2Ω, 3Ω and 6Ω are connected in parallel. (a) Calculate the equivalent resistance. (b) If a 12V battery is connected across this combination, find the current through the 6Ω resistor.
modelAnswer: (a) 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6 = 6/6 = 1. So R = 1Ω. (b) In parallel, same voltage (12V) across each resistor. Current through 6Ω = V/R = 12/6 = 2 A.
keyPoints: Parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3
Current through 6Ω = 12/6 = 2A (same voltage in parallel)

subject: Physics
text: State the principle of conservation of energy and illustrate it with the example of a simple pendulum.
modelAnswer: Principle of conservation of energy: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another. The total mechanical energy of an isolated system remains constant. In a simple pendulum: at the highest point (amplitude), all energy is potential (KE=0). At the lowest point (mean position), all energy is kinetic (PE=0). At intermediate points, energy is partly KE and partly PE, but total remains constant.
keyPoints: Total energy is conserved; not created or destroyed
Pendulum: highest point → all PE; lowest point → all KE
At any point: KE + PE = constant (total mechanical energy)

subject: Physics
text: A convex lens of focal length 15 cm forms an image of an object placed 30 cm from the lens. (a) Using the lens formula, find the image distance. (b) State the nature and size of the image relative to the object.
modelAnswer: (a) Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. Here u = −30 cm, f = +15 cm. 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/15 + 1/(−30) = 2/30 − 1/30 = 1/30. So v = +30 cm. (b) Image is real (v positive), inverted, same size as object (magnification = v/u = 30/30 = 1). Object is at 2F — image forms at 2F on other side.
keyPoints: Real, inverted image when v is positive for convex lens
Object at 2F → image at 2F, same size (m = 1)

subject: Physics
text: Distinguish between EMF and terminal voltage of a cell. Why is terminal voltage always less than EMF when current is drawn?
modelAnswer: EMF (electromotive force): the energy supplied by the cell per unit charge to drive current through the complete circuit (including internal resistance). Terminal voltage: the potential difference across the terminals of the cell when current flows (measured externally). Terminal voltage = EMF − I×r (where I = current, r = internal resistance). It is always less than EMF because some energy is used to overcome internal resistance of the cell.
keyPoints: EMF: energy/charge for complete circuit (open circuit voltage)
Terminal voltage = EMF − Ir (voltage drop across internal resistance)
Terminal V < EMF because of voltage drop across internal resistance

subject: Physics
text: Explain: (a) Why does the pitch of a sound from a vibrating column of air in a closed-end cylinder increase as you make the cylinder shorter? (b) Name and explain one characteristic of sound that depends on frequency.
modelAnswer: (a) In a closed-end cylinder, the fundamental frequency = v/4L (where v = speed of sound, L = length). As L decreases, frequency increases, hence pitch increases. Shorter column → higher natural frequency → higher pitch. (b) Pitch: the characteristic that allows us to classify a sound as high or low. It depends directly on frequency — higher frequency = higher pitch. Pitch is what we perceive subjectively as the 'shrillness' of a sound.
keyPoints: Closed cylinder: f = v/4L; shorter L → higher f → higher pitch
Pitch: subjective perception corresponding to frequency
Higher frequency → higher pitch

subject: Physics
text: (a) Define the term 'watt' as a unit of power. (b) Express it in terms of joule and second.
modelAnswer: (a) One watt (1 W) is the power of a machine that does one joule of work per second. It is the SI unit of power. (b) 1 W = 1 J/s = 1 J s⁻¹. Power = Work done / Time taken.
keyPoints: Watt = 1 J/s (one joule per second)
SI unit of power
1 kW = 1000 W; 1 horsepower ≈ 746 W

subject: Physics
text: Explain why: (a) the sky appears blue during the day. (b) the sun appears red at sunrise and sunset. (c) Danger signals are red in colour.
modelAnswer: (a) Blue sky: Sunlight undergoes Rayleigh scattering by air molecules. Blue light (short wavelength) scatters much more than red light (long wavelength). Scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all directions → sky appears blue. (b) Red sunrise/sunset: Light travels through more atmosphere at these times. Blue is scattered away over the long path; only longer wavelength red/orange light reaches our eyes directly. (c) Red signals: Red has the longest wavelength among visible colours and is scattered least by fog, rain, and dust — it can be seen from greatest distance.
keyPoints: Blue sky: Rayleigh scattering, blue (short λ) scattered most
Red sunrise/sunset: blue scattered away, red (long λ) transmitted
Red signals: longest wavelength, scattered least, visible at greatest distance

subject: Physics
text: Explain why: (a) Evaporation causes cooling. (b) Evaporation is faster on a windy day.
modelAnswer: (a) During evaporation, faster-moving (higher energy) molecules escape from the liquid surface. The remaining liquid is left with molecules of lower average kinetic energy, so its temperature decreases — the liquid cools. The heat is taken from the surroundings (latent heat of vaporization). (b) On a windy day, water vapour is continuously removed from near the liquid surface, reducing humidity. This maintains a large difference in vapour pressure/concentration, so molecules can escape more easily and continuously → faster evaporation.
keyPoints: Evaporation: high energy molecules escape → average KE of liquid decreases → cooling
Latent heat of vaporization is absorbed from surroundings
Wind: removes vapour, reduces humidity → faster evaporation rate

subject: Physics
text: Draw a labelled diagram of a block-and-tackle system with 3 pulleys in the lower block. State its velocity ratio.
modelAnswer: A block-and-tackle with 3 movable pulleys in the lower block has strings supporting the lower block — each pulley in lower block has 2 rope segments supporting it. Velocity Ratio (VR) = total number of rope segments supporting the lower block = 6 (if 3 pulleys in lower block, 6 rope segments). In general, VR = 2n where n = number of pulleys in lower block.
keyPoints: VR = number of rope segments supporting movable block
3 pulleys in lower block → VR = 6
MA (ideal) = VR when efficiency = 100%

subject: Physics
text: With respect to household wiring: (a) What is the function of fuse? (b) Why is the fuse always connected in the live wire? (c) State what happens when the fuse in a circuit 'blows'.
modelAnswer: (a) Fuse is a safety device that melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds a safe limit (its rated value), protecting appliances and wiring from damage due to overloading or short circuit. (b) Fuse is in the live wire so that when it blows, the appliance is completely cut off from the high-voltage live supply — otherwise the appliance chassis could remain at a dangerous potential even when 'off'. (c) When fuse blows: the fuse wire melts due to excessive heat (I²Rt), the circuit breaks (becomes open), no current flows, and the appliance stops working.
keyPoints: Fuse: safety device; melts when I exceeds rated value → breaks circuit
Always in live wire: ensures appliance is disconnected from high potential
Blown fuse: fuse wire melts → open circuit → appliance stops

subject: Physics
text: (a) Distinguish between alpha, beta and gamma radiations based on charge. (b) Which radiation is most penetrating?
modelAnswer: (a) Alpha (α): positively charged (+2, helium nucleus); Beta (β): negatively charged (−1, fast electron); Gamma (γ): no charge (electromagnetic radiation). (b) Gamma radiation is most penetrating — it can pass through several centimetres of lead or metres of concrete. Alpha is least penetrating (stopped by paper).
keyPoints: α: charge +2 (helium nucleus); least penetrating (stopped by paper)
β: charge −1 (fast electron); moderate penetration (stopped by Al sheet)
γ: no charge (EM radiation); most penetrating (stopped by thick lead)

subject: Physics
text: Define latent heat of fusion. The latent heat of fusion of ice is 336 J/g. How much heat is required to melt 500 g of ice at 0°C?
modelAnswer: Latent heat of fusion: the quantity of heat required to convert unit mass of a solid into liquid at constant temperature (its melting point). Q = mL = 500 × 336 = 168,000 J = 168 kJ.
keyPoints: Latent heat of fusion: heat to melt 1g/1kg at melting point (no temp change)
Q = mL

subject: Physics
text: Define refractive index. A ray of light travels from glass (refractive index 1.5) to air. Find the critical angle.
modelAnswer: Refractive index (n): the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in the medium: n = c/v. Also n = sin(angle of incidence) / sin(angle of refraction) for light going from medium to air. Critical angle C: sin C = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 2/3 = 0.667. C = sin⁻¹(0.667) ≈ 41.8°.
keyPoints: Refractive index n = c/v = sin i / sin r
Critical angle: sin C = 1/n
For glass (n=1.5): sin C = 1/1.5 → C ≈ 41.8°

subject: Physics
text: Distinguish between potential energy and kinetic energy. Calculate the kinetic energy of a body of mass 5 kg moving with a velocity of 10 m/s.
modelAnswer: Potential energy: energy stored in a body due to its position or state (e.g., gravitational PE = mgh). Kinetic energy: energy possessed by a body due to its motion (KE = ½mv²). KE = ½ × 5 × 10² = ½ × 5 × 100 = 250 J.
keyPoints: PE: stored energy due to position/state; PE = mgh
KE: energy due to motion; KE = ½mv²

subject: Physics
text: State any two differences between transverse waves and longitudinal waves.
modelAnswer: (i) Transverse waves: particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. Longitudinal waves: particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation. (ii) Transverse waves have crests and troughs; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions. Examples: transverse — light waves; longitudinal — sound waves.
keyPoints: Transverse: vibration ⊥ propagation; crests and troughs
Longitudinal: vibration ∥ propagation; compressions and rarefactions
Sound = longitudinal; Light = transverse

subject: Physics
text: Name the class of lever and give one example for each: (a) load between fulcrum and effort (b) effort between fulcrum and load.
modelAnswer: (a) Class II lever: load between fulcrum and effort. MA > 1 always. Example: wheelbarrow, bottle opener, nutcracker. (b) Class III lever: effort between fulcrum and load. MA < 1 always. Example: forceps, tweezers, sugar tongs, fishing rod.
keyPoints: Class II: F-L-E arrangement; MA > 1; example: wheelbarrow
Class III: F-E-L arrangement; MA < 1; example: forceps
Class I: L-F-E or E-F-L; MA can be > or < 1; example: seesaw

subject: Physics
text: State Ohm's law. A resistor of 10Ω is connected in series with a 5Ω resistor across a 30V supply. (a) Find the equivalent resistance. (b) Find the current flowing. (c) Find the voltage across the 5Ω resistor.
modelAnswer: Ohm's Law: At constant temperature, current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it: V = IR. (a) Series: R_eq = 10+5 = 15Ω. (b) I = V/R = 30/15 = 2A. (c) V₅Ω = I×R = 2×5 = 10V.
keyPoints: Ohm's Law: V = IR (constant temp)
Series resistance: R_eq = R1+R2 = 15Ω

subject: Physics
text: Explain: (a) What is radioactive decay? (b) Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion. (c) State one similarity between fission and fusion.
modelAnswer: (a) Radioactive decay: spontaneous disintegration of an unstable nucleus emitting alpha, beta, or gamma radiation to achieve stability. It cannot be controlled by physical/chemical means. (b) Fission: heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei releasing energy (e.g., U-235 + neutron → two medium nuclei + neutrons). Fusion: two light nuclei combine to form one heavier nucleus releasing energy (e.g., H + H → He). Fission needs slow neutrons; fusion requires very high temperature. (c) Both fission and fusion release enormous amounts of nuclear energy and are accompanied by a loss of mass (mass defect converted to energy by E=mc²).
keyPoints: Radioactive decay: spontaneous emission of α/β/γ to achieve stability
Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235); Fusion: light nuclei combine (H→He)
Both release massive energy; involve mass defect (E=mc²)

subject: Physics
text: Explain three ways by which heat can be transferred. Give one example of each.
modelAnswer: (a) Conduction: transfer of heat through a solid material by particle-to-particle vibration without actual movement of particles. Example: metal rod heated at one end. (b) Convection: transfer of heat through fluids (liquid/gas) by actual movement of particles (convection currents). Example: water heated in a beaker. (c) Radiation: transfer of heat without any medium as electromagnetic waves. Example: heat from the Sun reaching Earth.
keyPoints: Conduction: solids; particle vibration; no bulk movement
Convection: fluids; actual particle movement (convection currents)
Radiation: no medium needed; electromagnetic waves (e.g. Sun's heat)

subject: Physics
text: Compare the images formed by a concave lens and a convex lens for an object placed beyond 2F. State nature, position and size for each.
modelAnswer: Convex lens (object beyond 2F): Image is real, inverted, diminished, formed between F and 2F on the other side. Concave lens (object anywhere): Image is always virtual, erect, diminished, formed between F and optical centre on the same side as the object. A concave lens cannot form a real image regardless of object position.
keyPoints: Convex (obj beyond 2F): real, inverted, diminished, between F and 2F
Concave lens: always virtual, erect, diminished, same side as object
Concave lens never forms real image
